description: I am a freshman high school student with a strong interest in rocketry, aerospace technology, engineering, and space exploration. I enjoy designing and experimenting with engineering concepts, particularly model rocketry, and have experience using CAD software such as Fusion 360 to create 3D models, including rocket components. I am passionate about learning how engineering and technology can solve real-world challenges and contribute to future space exploration.
summary: Trajectory is a free rocket designer and flight simulator that runs in a web browser. For NASA Space Apps 2026 I added a Space Mission Design Game mode. You pick one of four NASA-style missions on Earth, Mars or the Moon, build a rocket that fits a payload and a budget, and fly it in 3D. A live checklist tracks highest point, payload weight, budget, stability and safe landing, with a plain-English hint for anything that fails. After landing, a debrief gives a score out of 1000 and an engineer rank. The simulator uses each world's gravity and air: Mars has very thin air, so a parachute barely helps, and the Moon has no air at all. A built-in tutorial teaches the game in a few minutes, and the whole event can be switched off to return to the plain rocket designer.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Trajectory is a free rocket designer and flight simulator that runs in a web browser, with nothing to install. For NASA Space Apps 2026 (challenge: Space Mission Design Game) I added a seasonal "NASA Mission Mode" that turns it into a mission design game.

You pick one of four missions: a Wallops ionosphere sounding probe (Earth, 1,200 m, 150 g payload, $350), a CubeSat technology demonstrator (Earth, 3,000 m, 500 g, $800), a Mars sample return ascent test (Mars, 5,000 m, 1 kg, $1,500) and a lunar hopper (Moon, 10,000 m, 2 kg, $2,500). You then build or edit a rocket. A floating checklist shows live whether it passes five checks: highest point, payload weight, budget, stability and safe landing. Each failing check says in plain words how to fix it. Then you fly it in 3D. The simulator uses the gravity and air of the chosen world. Mars has air about 60 times thinner than Earth's, so a parachute barely slows a rocket. The Moon has no air, so there is no drag, no steering and no parachute, and that mission is a purely ballistic hop. After landing, a debrief shows pass or fail for each requirement, flight numbers (highest altitude, top speed, strongest acceleration, flight time), a score out of 1000 and an engineer rank. A built-in "How to play" tutorial explains every step, and a "Load ready-made design" button starts you from a rocket that already passes the mission.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Mission design is about trade-offs: a bigger motor goes higher but costs more, more payload needs more thrust, and a rocket that is too light at the front tumbles. The game lets anyone, including students with no engineering background, feel those trade-offs in a few minutes and see how the same rocket behaves on three different worlds. It is aimed at students, teachers and hobby rocketeers, and it is free and works on any computer with a browser.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js with react-three-fiber for the 3D scenes, zustand for state, and Vitest (more than 300 automated tests). The flight simulator is my own: 3 degrees of freedom, RK4 integration, thrust curves, wind, parachutes and staging, running in a Web Worker. It is hosted as a static website. Rocket motor thrust curves come from ThrustCurve.org (718 motors). Planet constants (gravity, air density, scale height) come from the NASA NSSDC planetary fact sheets, and the drag model uses published NASA nose-cone drag data (NASA TR R-100) and fin flutter limits (NACA TN 4197). I built this with the help of Claude Code, an AI coding assistant from Anthropic, under my direction: I chose the features and missions, and reviewed and tested the results. No AI model runs inside the app.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It turns a serious engineering tool into a game with a story (four missions, an engineer rank, a score out of 1000) and makes the physics of different worlds something you can see and feel: the same parachute that saves a rocket on Earth barely works on Mars and is useless on the Moon. It also teaches by doing, with a guided tutorial that has buttons that perform each step for you. The event is built as one removable module behind a single switch, so after the event the app goes back to being the plain rocket designer.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Making it understandable for beginners (plain-English hints, a tutorial, a ready-made design for every mission); making every mission winnable but not trivial (each was checked by an automated test); keeping the physics honest for each world; and keeping the event isolated so it cannot break the main app.

LIMITS

The flight model was checked against OpenRocket on Earth (122 designs, highest point within 5% on all of them). It has not been checked against real flights, or against any flight on Mars or the Moon. Mars and Moon flights use a simple exponential atmosphere and constant gravity. Mission targets, budgets and the price list are game rules, not real NASA requirements, and scores come from this app's model.
